newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: TENNIS-CAPRIATI SOBS AFTER COMEBACK HITS DEAD END.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-CAPRIATI SOBS AFTER COMEBACK HITS DEAD END.

text.p: Former child star Jennifer Capriati broke down in tears on Tuesday after being dumped out in the first round on her Australian Open comeback.

Four years after her last appearance in Melbourne, when she reached the quarter-finals at the age of 16, Capriati was beaten 6-2 3-6 6-4 by fellow American Jolene Watanabe in a performance which disappointed a large crowd of fans.

There were no tears for Swiss starlet Martina Hingis, the teenager who replaced Capriati as the sport's latest prodigy, but the 16-year-old received a warning for racquet abuse during her 6-1 7-5 defeat of German veteran Barbara Rittner.
After reaching the final of a Sydney warm-up tournament on Saturday only to lose to Hingis, Capriati had been expected to enjoy a straightforward passage through to the second round.
But Watanabe, a 28-year-old who has never advanced beyond the first round of the Australian grand slam, was able to sit out the match on the baseline and watch Capriati throw it away.
"I was pretty disappointed. I didn't think I was playing nearly as well as last week," Capriati told a news conference.

Asked how she felt about the warm support from Australian fans, Capriati started to reply "just being out there and hearing the crowd..." but burst into tears, sobbing heavily before being escorted from the room by tour officials.
Capriati reached the last eight here at the age of 15 in 1992 and again the following year. After falling prey to teenage burn-out, she has begun the second comeback of her career.
Hingis, seen as the natural successor to world number one Steffi Graf, was more fortunate, but still had a frustrating time against Rittner.
Hingis was handed the warning from the umpire for throwing her racquet into the net after a service break against her in the second set led to a string of errors.
Hingis had strolled through the first set but Rittner lifted her game in a see-sawing second set in which most of the games went against serve.
Hingis at one point trailed 1-4 but won 11 straight points to level the scores and survived three break points in the 12th game in her final scare of the match.
Hingis has beaten both Graf and the injured world number two and 1996 Australian Open champion Monica Seles over the past year.
With Seles absent from the Open because of a broken finger, Hingis is seen as the player best equipped to prevent Graf winning a fifth Australian title.

In other action on a sweltering but blustery second day, German Anke Huber, the fifth seed and a losing finalist in Melbourne last year, recovered from a disastrous start to beat American Amy Frazier 0-6 6-2 7-5.
"I guess I didn't wake up. I don't know what happened," Huber said. "The wind was very difficult to play and I think it's not possible to play great tennis (in those conditions)."
In the men's singles, three lower seeds advanced without dropping a set between them.

South African Wayne Ferreira, seeded eight, overpowered clay court specialist Carlos Costa of Spain 6-3 6-2 6-2, while ninth seeded Chilean Marcelo Rios sent experienced Petr Korda of the Czech Republic packing 7-6 (7-4) 6-3 6-3 on centre court.
Sixteenth seed Alberto Berasategui of Spain thrashed Australian Todd Larkham 6-1 6-2 6-4 on an outside court.
